results.authors: Montalban X, Lebrun-Frenay C, Oh J, et al.
results.key_findings: Five regions for dissemination in space (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve). The optic nerve can be shown by MRI, OCT or VEP. The kappa free light chain index is accepted alongside CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands. The central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions are supporting MRI markers.

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
Do not accept carpal tunnel syndrome as the cause of the earlier right hand and forearm numbness: it was never confirmed and the residual non-dermatomal sensory loss is central
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF.

Exclude urinary tract infection (urinalysis and culture) before steroids, then give high-dose methylprednisolone for the disabling relapse (left optic neuritis 20/80 with left leg weakness and urgency): IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days as an inpatient or oral 500 mg daily for 5 days; consider plasma exchange if severe deficits do not respond.

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (two attacks in 8 months, enhancing brain, optic nerve and cord lesions, lesions in 5 of 5 regions), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception.

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, check full blood count with lymphocyte count, liver function, HBsAg and anti-HBc, hepatitis C, HIV and VZV IgG, and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before treatment starts
Measure the post-void residual for the urgency with near-incontinence: offer an antimuscarinic if the residual is low, and intermittent self-catheterisation if it is above 100 mL.
Explain the heat-related transient worsening she reports (Uhthoff phenomenon), and review vitamin D supplementation for the low 25-OH level (16 ng/mL on 2000 IU daily) as general health advice.

key_clinical_evidence: Day-5 painful left optic neuritis (acuity 20/80, left RAPD, Ishihara 4/14, normal disc) with an enhancing swollen 14 mm retrobulbar segment of the left optic nerve and a prolonged left P100 (126 ms).

Concurrent left-sided myelopathy (left hip and knee weakness, left Babinski sign, urgency, Lhermitte sign) matched by the faintly enhancing left C3-C4 lesion; left heel-to-shin ataxia matches the left middle cerebellar peduncle lesion.

DIS: 5 of 5 regions: periventricular (ovoid lesions, two enhancing), juxtacortical (left frontal), infratentorial (left middle cerebellar peduncle), spinal cord (C3-C4, T6-T7), optic nerve (left). With five regions no separate DIT or CSF is needed; enhancing and non-enhancing lesions also coexist.
Prior episode 8 months ago: 3 weeks of right hand and forearm numbness labelled carpal tunnel syndrome without nerve conduction studies, with residual non-dermatomal sensory loss.
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay, short eccentric cord lesions and five CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (kFLC index 52.3) argue against NMOSD and MOGAD.
Low 25-OH vitamin D (16 ng/mL) despite supplementation is a risk factor and comorbidity; it does not explain the lesions.

patient.history_present_illness: This 24-year-old right-handed woman presents to the emergency department with a 5-day history of progressive vision loss in the left eye accompanied by retro-orbital pain that worsens with eye movement. She first noticed mild blurring of vision in the left eye while driving to work on Monday morning. Over the following 48 hours, the blurriness worsened and she noticed that colors appeared washed out when viewed with the left eye alone, particularly reds which appeared more grey. By the third day, she developed a dull, aching retro-orbital pain on the left side that was exacerbated by lateral and upward gaze. She describes the pain as a deep pressure behind the eye, rated 5 out of 10, constant but worse with eye movement. Her visual acuity has continued to decline, and she reports significant difficulty reading with the affected eye. Concurrently, over the past 10 days, she has noticed progressive weakness and heaviness in her left leg. She initially attributed this to fatigue from a particularly busy week at work but became concerned when she tripped twice ascending stairs and noticed her left foot dragging. She also reports new-onset urinary urgency over the past two weeks, with several episodes of near-incontinence that are distressing to her. She has had to limit fluid intake and plan bathroom access carefully. When asked about prior neurological symptoms, she recalls an episode approximately 8 months ago when her right hand and forearm became numb and tingly, lasting about 3 weeks before gradually resolving. She was told this was likely carpal tunnel syndrome, though no nerve conduction studies were performed. She also mentions that for the past several months she has experienced unusual fatigue that she cannot attribute to any cause, and that since the hand episode the tingling in her right hand returns for a while after hot showers, a phenomenon she finds peculiar. She has had no recent infections, fevers, headaches, seizures, or changes in speech. There is no history of recent travel or tick bites. She reports that her maternal aunt was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in her mid-30s.

neurological_exam.additional: Lhermitte sign present: electric shock sensation radiating down the spine and into the legs upon neck flexion. Patient reports heat-related return of right hand tingling after hot showers (Uhthoff phenomenon).

Color vision impaired in the left eye: only 4/14 Ishihara plates identified correctly (right eye 14/14). Optic discs normal on fundoscopy, with no swelling or pallor. Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. No facial weakness. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Ambulates independently. Mild left leg circumduction noted. Tandem gait mildly impaired with two missteps over 10 paces. Romberg sign positive with eyes closed.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech is fluent without dysarthria or paraphasic errors. Attention and concentration intact, able to spell WORLD backwards. Short-term memory intact: 3/3 objects recalled at 5 minutes. Fund of knowledge appropriate for education level.
neurological_exam.motor: Tone normal in all four extremities. Strength 5/5 in bilateral upper extremities. Left hip flexion 4+/5, left knee extension 4+/5, left ankle dorsiflexion 5/5. Right lower extremity strength 5/5 throughout. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar reflexes 3+ bilaterally (brisk). Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Left Babinski sign (extensor plantar response) present. Right plantar response flexor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Decreased vibration sense in the left great toe compared to the right. Decreased light touch and pinprick sensation over the right forearm and hand in a non-dermatomal pattern. Temperature sensation intact. Joint position sense intact throughout.
